title: Cheaper machines below it, stronger ones behind it
lede: 3DO had a year’s head start on the 32-bit consoles. It spent that year at the highest price in the shop, and the companies that followed sold their own hardware at prices they chose.

blocks.title: What a console cost, 1993–1994
blocks.subtitle: Prices as reported by The New York Times. The Saturn and PlayStation prices are Japanese launch prices converted by the Times.

items.label: Philips CD-i, January 1993
items.note: A CD player for the television, not a 32-bit console[^19]

blocks.source: The New York Times, January 8, 1993[^19], September 9, 1993[^20] and December 11, 1994[^23].

blocks.title: One 3DO for the price of nearly eight 16-bit consoles

unit.label: the cheapest Sega or Nintendo system at the time[^23]

blocks.equation: $699 ÷ $89 ≈ 7.9, shown as 8. Both prices are from the same New York Times article.[^23]

blocks.title: Who won, who died
blocks.subtitle: The CD-based machines of 1993–1995, with the one sales figure our sources give for each.

items.name: 3DO Interactive Multiplayer
items.text: Matsushita’s count, eleven months after launch: 200,000 in Japan and 100,000 elsewhere. Every licensee had stopped making it by 1996.[^23][^1]

items.name: Sega Saturn
items.text: Sold out in Japan after its November 22, 1994 launch. Reached the United States in 1995.[^23][^1]

items.name: Sony PlayStation
items.text: Sony’s entire first Japanese shipment, from December 3, 1994. Reached the United States in 1995. 3DO was publishing games for it by 1999.[^23][^1][^5]

items.name: Atari Jaguar
items.text: The Times wrote in December 1994 that 1995 would be a battle “that only two or three contestants will survive,” and named [Atari](/atari/)’s machine among them.[^23]

items.name: Philips CD-i
items.text: Philips was spending more than $25M on advertising its $600 player when 3DO was unveiled.[^19]

blocks.source: The New York Times[^19][^23] and 3DO’s 10-K filings[^1][^5]. The figures are from different dates and markets and are not directly comparable. That the Saturn, Jaguar and CD-i were later discontinued and that the PlayStation line continues is general knowledge.

right.name: The incumbents
right.tag: Sega and Nintendo sold their own hardware

blocks.source: The New York Times, December 11, 1994[^23], and 3DO’s 10-K for fiscal 1996[^1]. The right-hand column describes the incumbents’ model as the Times described it, not audited figures.

blocks.text: The [64-bit based gaming] market has matured and it is difficult to make a fresh entry.
